title: Algorithms and Problem Solving
content:
Algorithms and Problem Solving

1. What is an Algorithm?

An algorithm is a step-by-step set of instructions for solving a problem or completing a task. It has a finite number of steps and always terminates.

Characteristics of a Good Algorithm

  • Input: Has zero or more inputs.
  • Output: Has one or more outputs.
  • Definiteness: Each step is clearly and precisely defined.
  • Finiteness: Always terminates (ends) after a finite number of steps.
  • Effectiveness: Each step is basic enough to be carried out.

2. Representing Algorithms

a. Pseudocode

Pseudocode is a way of writing algorithms using simple English-like statements without following the exact syntax of any programming language.
Common pseudocode keywords: START, STOP, INPUT, OUTPUT/PRINT, IF...THEN...ELSE...ENDIF, WHILE...DO...ENDWHILE, FOR...TO...NEXT, SET, READ, WRITE

b. Flowcharts

SymbolNameUsed For
Oval / Rounded rectangleTerminalStart and End
RectangleProcessActions and calculations
ParallelogramInput/OutputInput and Output
Diamond (Rhombus)DecisionConditions (Yes/No)
ArrowFlow lineDirection of flow

3. Control Structures

a. Sequence

Instructions executed one after another in order.

b. Selection (Conditional)

Execute different instructions based on a condition.

Pseudocode example:
IF score >= 50 THEN
   PRINT "Pass"
ELSE
   PRINT "Fail"
ENDIF

c. Iteration (Loops)

WHILE loop:
WHILE count <= 10 DO
   PRINT count
   SET count = count + 1
ENDWHILE

FOR loop:
FOR i = 1 TO 5
   PRINT i
NEXT i

4. Common Algorithms

Swap Algorithm

SET temp = A
SET A = B
SET B = temp

Finding Maximum

SET max = list[1]
FOR i = 2 TO n
  IF list[i] > max THEN
    SET max = list[i]
  ENDIF
NEXT i

Linear Search

SET found = FALSE
FOR i = 1 TO n
  IF list[i] = target THEN
    SET found = TRUE
  ENDIF
NEXT i

Bubble Sort

Repeatedly compare adjacent elements and swap if out of order, until no swaps are needed.

title: Programming Languages and Paradigms
content:
Programming Languages and Paradigms

1. Programming Languages

A programming language is a formal language comprising a set of instructions that produce various kinds of output and implement algorithms.

Low-Level Languages

  • Machine Language (1GL): Binary code (0s and 1s). Directly understood by CPU. Very fast but difficult to write.
  • Assembly Language (2GL): Uses mnemonics (e.g., ADD, MOV, LOAD). Needs an assembler to translate to machine code.

High-Level Languages (3GL and above)

  • Close to human language. Examples: Python, Java, C, C++, Pascal, BASIC.
  • Portable (can run on different hardware with little modification).
  • Must be translated to machine code by a compiler or interpreter.

2. Language Translators

TranslatorDescriptionProduces
AssemblerTranslates assembly language to machine codeMachine code
CompilerTranslates entire source code at once; produces object codeExecutable file
InterpreterTranslates and executes one line at a timeNo separate file

3. Programming Paradigms

ParadigmDescriptionLanguages
Procedural / ImperativePrograms as sequences of instructions; uses procedures/functionsC, Pascal, BASIC
Object-Oriented (OOP)Organises code into objects with properties and methodsJava, Python, C++
FunctionalPrograms as mathematical functions; avoids changing stateHaskell, Erlang
DeclarativeDescribes what to do, not how to do itSQL, HTML

4. Data Types

Data TypeDescriptionExample
IntegerWhole numbers (no decimal)5, -3, 0
Real/FloatNumbers with decimal point3.14, -2.5
BooleanTrue or False onlyTrue, False
Character (Char)Single character'A', '5'
StringSequence of characters"Hello"

5. Program Errors

  • Syntax Error: Code breaks grammar rules of the language. Caught by compiler/interpreter. Example: missing semicolon.
  • Logic Error: Program runs but produces wrong output. The algorithm/reasoning is incorrect. Hardest to find.
  • Runtime Error: Error that occurs during execution. Example: dividing by zero, accessing invalid memory.

title: Data Structures
content:
Data Structures

A data structure is a way of organising and storing data in a computer so that it can be accessed and modified efficiently.

Simple Data Types

  • Integer: Whole numbers (e.g., 5, -10).
  • Real/Float: Numbers with decimals (e.g., 3.14).
  • Boolean: True or False.
  • Character: Single character (e.g., 'A').
  • String: Sequence of characters (e.g., "GHS Mbonjo").

Composite Data Structures

Arrays

An array is a collection of elements of the same data type stored at contiguous memory locations and accessed by index.

1D Array: A list. Example: marks[1..5] = [70, 65, 80, 55, 90]

2D Array: A table/matrix. Example: grid[row][column]

Records

A record is a collection of related fields that can be of different data types, representing one entity.

Example: Student record = {Name: String, Age: Integer, Pass: Boolean}

Lists

An ordered collection of items (like arrays but can grow/shrink).

Queues

FIFO (First In, First Out) structure. Items added at rear, removed from front. Example: printer queue.

Stacks

LIFO (Last In, First Out) structure. Items added and removed from the top only. Example: undo operations.

Difference: Data Type vs Data Structure

FeatureData TypeData Structure
DefinitionClassification of data (what kind of value)Way of organising/storing multiple data items
ExamplesInteger, String, BooleanArray, Stack, Queue, Record
ComplexitySimple / PrimitiveComposite / Complex
